report.source_text: Because chemotherapy for ECD risked worsening infection of the CNS with T. gondii, the plan was to initiate treatment with anti-Toxoplasma drugs first, and the patient was transferred to another hospital designated for infectious diseases. After transfer, the administration of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid was initiated. However, the patient showed no improvement of any neurologic symptoms, and psychiatric symptoms, such as excited state, hallucination, delusion, and cognitive decline, were gradually exacerbated. MRI of the brain after anti-Toxoplasma treatment showed no marked changes (Fig. 1C).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 63-year-old man presented with a 29-month history of dizziness and was found on gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI to have multiple small enhancing nodules in bilateral cerebrum, brainstem, and cerebellum, with corresponding high-intensity lesions on FLAIR imaging. Biopsy of a right frontal lobe subcortical mass revealed foamy macrophages that were CD68-positive, CD163-positive, and CD1a-negative on immunohistochemistry, with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by DNA sequencing. Systemic imaging demonstrated bone involvement (markedly increased 99mTc-MDP uptake around both knees with sclerotic lesions on CT) and retroperitoneal/perivascular soft-tissue infiltration around the descending thoracic aorta and left kidney on contrast-enhanced CT. A concurrent Toxoplasma gondii CNS infection was identified (serum IgG antibody positive at 61.6 U/mL, CSF PCR positive in 1 of 3 samples, though brain biopsy showed no T. gondii organisms). CSF analysis showed mild protein elevation (68 mg/dL) with normal cell counts and glucose. Anti-Toxoplasma therapy (pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, folinic acid) was initiated but resulted in no neurologic improvement and worsening psychiatric symptoms, with brain MRI showing no marked changes. The constellation of multifocal CNS lesions, characteristic histopathology (foamy macrophages), immunophenotype (CD68+/CD163+/CD1a-), BRAF V600E mutation, and systemic involvement (bone and retroperitoneal infiltration) confirmed the diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease.
